Brain aging

Several rodent experiments reported improved learning or memory measures after near-infrared PBM. Cytochrome-c-oxidase activity also decreased in some regions, so the tissue-marker response was not uniformly aligned with behavioral outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several rodent experiments reported improved learning or memory measures after near-infrared PBM. Cytochrome-c-oxidase activity also decreased in some regions, so the tissue-marker response was not uniformly aligned with behavioral outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact brain-aging category contains six unique animal publications: four rat studies and two mouse studies. They examine different aging models and treatment schedules, so six titles do not equal six replications of one protocol. Two recent Spanish rat papers come from a related research program, but the database does not establish whether their animal samples overlap. One mouse paper uses an aged Alzheimer-transgenic model, which combines aging with disease pathology.

Human and clinical evidence

No human study is classified in the brain-aging category. The available evidence therefore concerns rodent memory, movement, and tissue measures rather than age-related cognitive decline in people.

Animal evidence

In a 2026 rat study, 810 nm near-infrared PBM delivered at different pulse frequencies produced frequency-dependent findings. Forty-hertz treatment improved learning speed in aged rats. The researchers also observed changes in synaptic, inflammatory, and cell-death markers; cytochrome-c-oxidase activity decreased in several measures, showing that not every tissue response moved in a simple “more activity” direction (Arias et al. 2026).

A related study in middle-aged rats reported improved spatial memory and cognitive flexibility after repeated PBM, without detected changes in anxiety-like behavior or locomotor activity. Cytochrome-c-oxidase activity again decreased in memory-related regions (Rodríguez-Fernández et al. 2026). Other records include an induced-aging mouse model with a dose-dependent response, chronic 810 nm rat experiments measuring mitochondrial and cell-survival signaling, and 670 nm red visible-light treatment that increased neural-stem-cell markers in aged Alzheimer-transgenic mice.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo publication is classified under brain aging. Cellular markers reported in the rat and mouse experiments were measured as part of those animal studies.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Most experiments used transcranial 810 nm near-infrared light. The recent rat papers compared pulsed stimulation at 5 and 40 Hz, with treatment over five days in young animals and up to 11 consecutive days in older animals. Other studies used 810 nm for 58 days or compared 8, 16, and 32 J/cm² in an induced-aging mouse model. One aged Alzheimer-transgenic model used 670 nm red visible LED light. These are varied animal protocols, not a dose-finding sequence that identifies a human treatment setting.

Interpretation

The rodent studies report improved learning or memory in selected aging models, alongside measurable but mixed brain-marker responses. The 40 Hz rat result and the repeated-treatment rat study give behavioral outcomes a favorable direction, while reduced cytochrome-c-oxidase activity shows that the mechanism is not captured by a single marker. Human studies are needed to determine whether these model findings translate to cognition in older adults.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for selected memory and neural-marker outcomes in rodent aging models No direct human evidence for age-related cognitive decline
Publications and records6 unique animal publications (rat; mouse)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Six publications report animal experiments, including recent rat studies with improved learning or memory measures and separate changes in brain markers. The findings come from related research groups and different aging models, while one transgenic mouse model also involves Alzheimer pathology. Independent replication across normal-aging models and controlled studies in older adults would be needed before drawing conclusions about human cognition.
